title: Counting Intervals
description: Learn to measure the distance between two notes by counting keys, and what each distance sounds like.

steps.title: Distance between notes
steps.description:
An interval is just the distance from one note to another. We measure it in semitones: one semitone is one key to the very next key, black or white.

Every chord and every melody is made of intervals, so once you can count them, a lot of theory stops being mysterious.

steps.title: The ones you'll meet most
steps.description:
Count the keys from the lower note to the upper one:

• 0, unison: the same note twice
• 1, minor 2nd: a sharp, tense rub
• 2, major 2nd: a whole step, like a scale moving along
• 3, minor 3rd: darker, a bit sad
• 4, major 3rd: bright and sunny
• 5, perfect 4th: open, like 'Here Comes the Bride'
• 7, perfect 5th: strong and hollow, like 'Twinkle, Twinkle'
• 12, octave: the same note, higher up

steps.title: A major 3rd
steps.description: Play C and E together. Count it: C, C#, D, D#, E. That's 4 semitones up. Hear how bright it is?
steps.hint: Middle C and the E two white keys up.

steps.title: A perfect 5th
steps.description: Now C and G together, 7 semitones apart. It's the sound of a rock power chord: open, solid, neither happy nor sad.
steps.hint: Middle C and the G four white keys up.

steps.title: Counting a 5th
steps.description: How many semitones are in a perfect 5th?

steps.title: Counting a 3rd
steps.description: And a major 3rd, how many semitones is that?
